qt: to the Commission Morten Løkkegaard (Renew) Subject:

In 2021, the Commission criticised the Danish conversion model for the European Baccalaureate (EB), in response to which Denmark changed its practice. However, according to Danish parents’ representatives at the European School, the Danish conversion model for EB students still places them at a disadvantage compared with both Danish upper secondary (STX) students and International Baccalaureate (IB) students when applying for higher education, owing, among other things, to the grade conversion and lack of access to an individual ‘Bonus A’ grading adjustment scheme. With the above in mind, and in the light of the attached note1: 1.

Does the Commission take the view that the current Danish grade conversion model for the European Baccalaureate ensures genuine equal treatment and is in line with Denmark’s obligations under the Convention defining the Statute of the European Schools of 21 June 1994?
What practical action will the Commission recommend that Denmark take to ensure that it fully delivers on its commitments?

Does the Commission think that the fact that EB students are not eligible for an individual Bonus A adjustment could put them at a disadvantage compared with Danish STX students, thus constituting discrimination in breach of the Convention defining the Statute of the European Schools of 21 June 1994?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.11.2026) In 2021, the Commission launched an infringement procedure as it considered that Denmark’s method for converting European Baccalaureate grades was incompatible with Article 5 of the Convention defining the Statute of the European Schools1, because it compared the European Schools’ single academic pathway with the full range of Danish upper-secondary programmes, rather than with the comparable academic pathway alone (STX). At the same time, the Commission’s assessment did not call into question the Danish statistical conversion methodology as such. The Commission found that the methodology, based on a comparison of the statistical distribution of grades obtained in the Danish and foreign or international systems in a given year, was applied consistently to all foreign and international certificates, including the European Baccalaureate, and did not in itself cause the unequal treatment referred to in Article 5 of the Convention. The Commission also noted that, although the Danish system does not grant individual Abonuses to holders of foreign or international certificates, it indirectly reflects that element by adjusting the scale so that the maximum converted Danish grade is 12.7 (12 x 1,06). The Commission considered that there were insufficient grounds to conclude that this approach constituted a breach of Article 5 of the Convention. During the infringement procedure, the Danish authorities accepted the Commission’s concerns and amended their grade conversion regulations so that European Baccalaureate diplomas are compared only with STX diplomas. In view of this, the Commission concluded that Denmark had complied with its obligations under Article 5 of the Convention and closed the procedure in 2024.
